slides.texte_overlay:
How to make a great first
impression on anyone
Have your hands free when you walk in. Coat off, bag down, drink in your left hand. You're ready to shake hands without awkward juggling.
Use their name once early and once at the end. "Nice to meet you, Anna" and "Great talking, Anna." Twice feels warm and personal. Ten times sounds like a sales trick, so keep it natural.
Ask about something they chose. Their job, their city, their dog. People light up when talking about decisions they made themselves.
Keep your first story short. Thirty seconds, one funny detail, then hand the conversation back. First impressions are about them, not your biography.
Bring something interesting into the room. I do five minutes a day of history, art or science, and a fun fact is the easiest way to be remembered warmly.
slides.texte_sophia: I do five minutes a day on a micro-learning app like the Sophia app. History, art, science. A fun fact is the easiest way to be remembered warmly.

slides.texte_overlay: Match their handshake, not your strongest grip. Firm, short, with eye contact. A good handshake feels balanced and friendly, never like a contest of strength.
Leave with a small promise and keep it. "I'll send you that book title tonight." Then send it. Follow-through turns a first impression into trust.
